name: Digital Science (Holtzbrinck Publishing Group), incl. Figshare
subcategory: commercial research-infrastructure group; Figshare general-purpose data repository (proprietary SaaS hosting openly licensed content), plus Dimensions, Altmetric, Overleaf, ReadCube, Symplectic
origin_detail: Figshare began as Mark Hahnel's personal tool for sharing the research outputs of his PhD in stem cell biology; Figshare Alpha launched in 2011 and V1 on 17 January 2012, a relaunch backed by Digital Science. Digital Science itself launched on 7 December 2010 in London as the technical division of Nature Publishing Group/Macmillan (founder Timo Hannay) and is run as an independent company by the Holtzbrinck Publishing Group, which also owns 53% of Springer Nature. Figshare is operated by Figshare LLP and branded 'a Digital Science solution'.
flagship_projects: Figshare.com (free individual repository, files up to 20 GB)
Figshare+ (2021, paid deposit of multi-TB datasets)
Overleaf (AGPL-3.0 Community Edition, proprietary Server Pro and SaaS)
ReadCube, Symplectic Elements, Writefull, Metaphactory, IFI CLAIMS
openness_notes: Figshare's code base is not open source and Figshare describes itself as a commercial vendor. Its openness is in the content and interfaces: most files are released CC BY and datasets CC0 (Wikipedia); the API is openly documented; and it supports DataCite DOIs, machine-readable metadata and OAI-PMH, with 'no vendor lock-in' on shared outputs. That is level 1 (only peripheral interfaces open; closed platform, corporate control). Elsewhere in the group, Overleaf is genuinely open core (AGPL-3.0 Community Edition, 18.4k GitHub stars, versus proprietary Server Pro and overleaf.com), and Dimensions has a free tier limited to publications and datasets; the rest of the portfolio is proprietary SaaS.

exit_events.note: Digital Science backed Figshare's January 2012 relaunch and Figshare is now 'part of Digital Science'; the stake, date of full ownership and terms were not found on fetched pages

risk_events: Open-science infrastructure owned by a publishing group: Digital Science's parent Holtzbrinck also owns 53% of Springer Nature
Jul 2026: CEO Daniel Hook (11 years) moved to a new Chief Scientific Officer role at Holtzbrinck; President Steve Leicht became CEO
Closed code means the platform cannot be forked or self-hosted if the owner changes course; mitigated by DOIs, an open API and CLOCKSS archiving of content
robustness: Commercially sustained (institutional subscriptions and Figshare+ charges) inside a large, long-lived family-owned media group, with public funding on top: a 2022 NIH Generalist Repository Ecosystem Initiative (GREI) award alongside Dryad, Mendeley Data, Dataverse, Zenodo, OSF and Vivli. Content is portable (DataCite DOIs, OAI-PMH, documented API) and CLOCKSS is an additional host, but the software is single-vendor and closed.
physical_science_relevance: Figshare is one of the generalist repositories that funders such as NIH recognise and a common home for publishers' supplementary data (PLOS integration since 2013). For a materials lab its free tier (20 GB files, CC0 datasets with DOIs) and Figshare+ (multi-TB) suit large microscopy, CT or process-monitoring datasets; for the Digital Alloy Lab that could include LPBF build logs and melt-pool imaging, though Zenodo offers similar terms on open-source, publicly run infrastructure. Digital Science's Overleaf (AGPL core) and Dimensions are also widely used for writing and literature analytics.
openness_effect_assessment: Open licences on content and free individual deposits drove Figshare's growth to over 8 million openly available research outputs and 150+ partner organisations by 2024, and earned it a place in NIH's GREI. Keeping the platform closed let Digital Science sell institutional repositories as SaaS, so Figshare is 'open science on closed infrastructure', unlike Zenodo (open-source InvenioRDM, CERN-operated).
key_takeaway: Digital Science shows the commercial route to open-science infrastructure: a publisher-owned group (Holtzbrinck) that backed a PhD student's data-sharing tool in 2012 and turned it into institutional SaaS, while keeping the content openly licensed and the code closed. Researchers get free, DOI-backed open data deposit; institutions and funders get a vendor, not a commons, so portability rests on DOIs and APIs rather than forkable code.
